title: PS-19 Precision agriculture in beef cattle production: Using GPS and activity monitors to assess beef bull behavior
content:
Abstract
Managing large scale beef cattle operations can be very challenging, posing difficulties in managing as well as sustaining large scale herds. Large scale rangeland cattle operations have operated for hundreds of years and oftentimes are operated on extremely large tracts of land. Using precision agriculture as a resource for managing beef cattle herds is a relatively new concept. To better our understanding of the applications of precision agriculture technologies we set out to conduct a preliminary study on the validity and usefulness of technology in beef production systems. Using GPS ear tags equipped with activity monitors, 163 range bulls in south central Montana were tagged and turned out into four breeding groups (yearlings, first calf heifers and two mature cow groups; mean pasture size of 3,130 ha). For this group of commercial range bulls we obtained or determined bull age, feet and leg scores, muscle scores, frame scores, and body condition scores at the start and end of the breeding season. Using company provided algorithms, the ear tags estimated heart rate, time spent grazing, resting, ruminating, and traveling. Mean and coefficient of variation (CV) for all animals were: 72.0 beats per minute (BPM; CV=11.0%), 8.2 h spent grazing (CV=16.1%), 7.8 h spent resting (CV=28.7%), 5.9 h spent ruminating (CV=25.3%), and 0.74 h spent traveling (CV=76.3%). We then calculated the correlation coefficient of all measured bull traits with the tag estimated bull activities. Muscle score was negatively correlated to heart rate (r = -0.29), positively correlated with time spent resting (r = 0.18), and negatively correlated with time spent traveling (r = -0.25). Frame score was negatively correlated with heart rate (r = -0.11) and negatively correlated with time spent resting (r = -0.12). Body condition score at the start of breeding season is positively correlated with time spent ruminating (r = 0.14), and negatively correlated with time spent traveling (r = -0.13). Bull age is negatively correlated with heart rate (r = -0.28), positively correlated with time spent resting (r = 0.29), negatively correlated with time spent ruminating (r = -0.19), and negatively correlated with time spent traveling (r = -0.26). In summary, our preliminary results suggest that GPS/activity monitor ear tag technology has potential to characterize range bull behavior on extensive landscapes, in turn enhancing beef cattle production systems. Future research at Montana State University will evaluate the application of this technology, applicability in extensive production environments, as well as accuracy of predicting animal behavior attributes.
